voiceover: Six facts about Jesus' empty tomb you've probably never heard. One. Jesus was buried by Joseph of Arimathea — a member of the very council that had handed him over. The Catholic scholar Raymond Brown, writing as a critical historian, judged a Christian invention of that detail almost inexplicable. Two. Jewish law required the executed to be buried before nightfall — and Josephus says the Jews took down and buried even the crucified before sunset. Three. In 1968, in a Jerusalem burial box, archaeologists found the heel bone of a crucified man named Yehohanan, the iron nail still driven through it. At least some victims of crucifixion in Jesus' city were given proper burial. Four. The earliest Jewish reply we can recover was that the disciples stole the body. Around 150, Justin Martyr records the charge, and around 200 Tertullian knows it too: an enemy polemic that explains the emptiness rather than denying it, traceable across a century. Five. The first witnesses were women — and the male apostles dismissed their report as an idle tale. They are the last witnesses anyone inventing the story would choose. Six. Mark's earliest account is strikingly plain: an open grave and frightened women — none of the guards, angelic choreography or spectacle later apocryphal gospels would heap on. Taken together, in all probability, the tomb was found empty. The real question is why.

scenes.vo: Six facts about Jesus' empty tomb you've probably never heard.

One. Jesus was buried by Joseph of Arimathea — a member of the very council that had handed him over. The Catholic scholar Raymond Brown, writing as a critical historian, judged a Christian invention of that detail almost inexplicable.
Two. Jewish law required the executed to be buried before nightfall — and Josephus says the Jews took down and buried even the crucified before sunset.

Three. In 1968, in a Jerusalem burial box, archaeologists found the heel bone of a crucified man named Yehohanan, the iron nail still driven through it. At least some victims of crucifixion in Jesus' city were given proper burial.

Four. The earliest Jewish reply we can recover was that the disciples stole the body. Around 150, Justin Martyr records the charge, and around 200 Tertullian knows it too: an enemy polemic that explains the emptiness rather than denying it, traceable across a century.
Five. The first witnesses were women — and the male apostles dismissed their report as an idle tale. They are the last witnesses anyone inventing the story would choose.
Six. Mark's earliest account is strikingly plain: an open grave and frightened women — none of the guards, angelic choreography or spectacle later apocryphal gospels would heap on.
Taken together, in all probability, the tomb was found empty. The real question is why.
